extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, filmmakers, and scholars interested in the thriller genre
extracted.subtask_description: Characteristics and conventions for creating or analysing thriller fiction (literature, film, and television), focusing on mood, suspense techniques, common themes, characters, and settings. Useful for writers, critics, and students learning what makes a work a thriller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary mood — suspenseful excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrillers are characterized and defined by the moods they elicit, giving their audiences heightened feelings of suspense, excitement, surprise, anticipation and anxiety. 'If it "thrills", it is a thriller.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The variety of thriller subgenres share a common ground in the intensity of emotions they create—apprehension, exhilaration, excitement, and breathlessness. A thriller that doesn't thrill is not doing its job (James Patterson quote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense — sustained tension and anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense is a crucial characteristic: pleasurable fascination and excitement mixed with apprehension, anticipation, and tension that develop from unpredictable, mysterious, and rousing events during the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective is sustained tension, surprise, and a constant sense of impending doom. Hitchcock's formulation: audience expects something bad and may have superior knowledge but is powerless to intervene. Suspense intertwines hope and anxiety (hope things will turn out, fear they may not). Aristotle's Poetics regards suspense as an important building block. Film music can enhance distrust and ominous uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of literary devices (red herrings, plot twists, unreliable narrators, cliffhangers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary devices such as red herrings, plot twists, unreliable narrators, and cliffhangers are used extensively in thrillers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices are employed to maintain audience engagement, mislead or reorient expectations, and build to climactic revelations or shocks. Examples include multiple plot twists and cliffhanger chapter endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Villain-driven plots and antagonist obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: A thriller is often a villain-driven plot, whereby they present obstacles that the protagonist or hero must overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The antagonist's actions create continual conflict and danger, driving the narrative forward and producing suspense as the protagonist struggles against these obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover-up or concealment of important information
rubrics_metrics.description: The cover-up of important information is a common element in thrillers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding or concealing facts from the protagonist (and sometimes from the audience) generates mystery and prolongs suspense; revelations are used for climactic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: High stakes and ticking-clock urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrillers typically have high stakes—life, national security, or other grave consequences—and often employ a ticking clock to raise urgency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots emphasize danger to the protagonist or larger threats (e.g., threats to countries), and time pressure increases tension and drives pacing toward a climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common themes and methods by subgenre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different thriller subgenres favor characteristic themes and methods: crime/action thrillers use ransoms, captivities, heists, revenge, kidnappings; mystery thrillers emphasize investigations and whodunit technique; psychological thrillers use plot twists, psychology, obsession and mind games; sci‑fi thrillers feature killing robots, mad scientists; horror thrillers include serial killers, stalking, deathtraps; paranoid thrillers include fringe theories, false accusations, paranoia; spy thrillers include espionage, conspiracies, assassins, electronic surveillance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subgenre-appropriate threats, plot mechanics, and thematic focus to meet readers' genre expectations while allowing variation and hybridization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character types and protagonist profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Thriller characters may include criminals, stalkers, assassins, innocent victims (often on the run), menaced women, psychotic individuals, sociopaths, agents, terrorists, police, escaped convicts, private eyes, people in twisted relationships, and world-weary men and women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagonists are frequently ordinary citizens unaccustomed to danger (though 'hard men' like police/detectives are common in crime/action thrillers). Female lead characters are increasingly common. Psychological thrillers often feature protagonists who must rely on mental resources, battling wits or their own equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmosphere, setting and placement of ordinary characters in danger
rubrics_metrics.description: An atmosphere of menace and sudden violence characterizes thrillers; tension arises when characters are placed in dangerous situations or traps from which escape seems impossible. Thrillers take place mostly in ordinary suburbs and cities, though exotic settings appear as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing resourceful but essentially ordinary heroes against determined villains in familiar settings heightens relatability and dread. Settings and atmosphere should reinforce the sense of peril and inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative expectation management (curiosity, surprise vs. suspense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense is contrasted with curiosity and surprise: the narrative's objective is to deliver sustained tension and surprise while managing what the audience knows versus what characters know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the hierarchy of knowledge (audience may know more than characters) to create suspense, and manipulate reveals to balance anticipation and shock. Employ pacing so final moments (however short) are most memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological interplay (hope and anxiety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense in thrillers is often intertwined with hope and anxiety—the hope that things will turn out all right for appropriate characters and the fear that they may not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate emotional investments so readers oscillate between expectation of safety and dread, deepening engagement with the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and genre awareness (use of established conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrillers draw on long-standing conventions and historical precedents (e.g., The Count of Monte Cristo, The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hitchcock films) that shaped suspense techniques, plot twists, and genre expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of canonical examples and evolution of subgenres helps creators choose conventions to emulate, subvert, or innovate while remaining recognizably within the thriller tradition.
